projects.title: StoveDetector
projects.summary: A sensor that notices when a stove has been left on and unattended, and sounds an alert before it becomes a fire.
body: A sensor that notices when a stove has been left on and unattended, and sounds an alert before it becomes a fire. Started as a personal safety fix (formerly "KitchenEye"); now a hardware startup heading into its first pilot homes.
Custom carrier board, Wi-Fi alerts, and a pre-pilot FCC compliance process I'm running myself.

projects.title: The Louis: MIDI Trumpet
projects.summary: An affordable MIDI trumpet built to look, feel and sound like the real thing, for under $150 in parts.
body: An affordable MIDI trumpet built to look, feel and sound like the real thing, so remote-learning students could practice without the cost or noise of an actual trumpet.
Real valve springs and mouthpiece, a 3D-printed body, an I2S mic reading the mouthpiece buzz, valve sensors, and a Raspberry Pi + Teensy for signal processing, all for under $150 in parts.
Inspired by David Baylies' Stella electronic trumpet. Our note-detection code builds on his open-source Stella code, and David advised us directly during development.
Senior capstone at Brown (ENGN 1001), April 2021.
Read the full write-up (32-page PDF) → Design, signal processing, testing and what we'd change.

projects.title: Future You: Affect Extension
projects.summary: A sensing plugin for MIT Media Lab's Future You that reads how you answer (face, voice and heart rate), not just what you type.
body: A sensing plugin for MIT Media Lab's Future You, where people talk with an AI simulation of their older self. Future You builds that persona only from what you type. The extension also watches how you answer: face (MediaPipe blendshapes), voice (pitch, loudness, pauses) and heart rate from a Bluetooth strap. The output is an affect profile and a persona prompt, so the future-self conversation knows which topics made you tense, energised, hesitant or calm.

Every feature is measured against your own 45-second resting baseline. It never outputs emotion labels, and your self-report overrides the sensors when they disagree. All sensing runs locally in the browser.

projects.title: Thermal Self-Observation
projects.summary: An exploratory thermal-camera study of surface warmth across my head, chest and body while I work at a laptop.
body: I want to use a thermal camera to observe warm spots across my head, chest and body while working at my laptop, and explore how those patterns change over a work session.
This is a concept, not a completed experiment. I plan to pair the thermal observations with my own notes about the experience.
Thermal images show surface temperature, not emotions or core body temperature, and clothing, room temperature, movement and camera position all affect the readings.

projects.title: Yale Shuttle Tracker
projects.summary: A live map, stop-by-stop arrival times and a trip planner for Yale's Downtowner shuttles, predicted from what the buses actually did.
body: A live map, stop-by-stop arrival times and a trip planner for Yale's Downtowner shuttles. It polls the shuttle GPS feed every 5 seconds and builds its own history of arrivals, dwell times and travel times between stops. Predictions are calibrated from what the buses actually did on that stretch of route at that hour and day of the week, not from the published timetable. The planner routes between any two points, including the walking legs.
A single Node service (Hono, SQLite) with a React front end, plus automated map and data checks that catch bad predictions before riders see them.

projects.title: UCG Asset Map
projects.summary: A shared mind map, map, calendar and directory of the help available to neighbors on the New Haven Green, edited live by a church team.
body: A shared workspace for United Church on the Green, built around one question: how can the church support neighbors on the New Haven Green who are experiencing homelessness and the effects of poverty? The team records every organization, service and idea as a card, and the same cards show up in four views: a mind map for thinking, a street map for where things are, a calendar for when they are open, and a directory for looking things up.

Everyone edits the same map at once. The map is a Yjs document synced over WebSockets, so two people can type in the same card, and edits made during a dropped connection stay on the device and are sent again when it returns. Every save is kept in a version history. Accounts are created with an invite code, and nothing is visible without signing in.
A Node server with a vanilla JS front end, bundled with esbuild and hosted on Fly.io. Every push to main is tested and deployed automatically.

screenshots.alt: Mind map view: the central question branches into groups such as New Haven nonprofits, which opens into organizations like Columbus House and the services each one offers.
Map view: organizations and services pinned on a street map of New Haven around the Green, with group filters in a sidebar.
Calendar view: a week of meals, food pantries and drop-in hours, color-coded by the kind of help.
Directory view: the same cards as a searchable, collapsible list, with the New Haven nonprofits group expanded.

projects.title: Agent Dashboard
projects.summary: One home base for my AI agents: ask once, it routes to the right specialist, and it only interrupts me when an agent needs me.
body: A private home base for the AI agents that help run my projects (built on OpenClaw). I type a request once and it goes to the right specialist: a local embedding model matches it against each agent's profile, with an LLM router as the fallback. Conversations are grouped by project, live work streams in as it happens, and anything an agent is blocked on (an approval, a question) lands in one Inbox, kept separate from the to-do list, so nothing nags unless it needs me.
A nightly cleanup asks each idle chat's agent to save what mattered before the chat is archived.
Plain Node and vanilla JS with no dependencies or build step. It runs locally only and talks to the OpenClaw Gateway over its WebSocket protocol with least-privilege access.

screenshots.alt: Home: one 'What would you like to work on?' box that auto-picks an agent, with five chats open side by side in named sections, each showing a one-line summary of the agent's latest reply. (Demo data.)

projects.title: Recursive Find
projects.summary: Ctrl+F, but recursive: a Chrome extension that searches the page you're on and every page it links to.
body: Ctrl+F, but recursive. A Chrome side-panel extension that searches the page you're on and every page it links to, down to a depth you choose. Results stream in live, sorted by hit count, with a preview of each match. Click one and the page opens scrolled to the highlighted text.

Plain text, whole-word or regex matching, with options for match case, same site only, and stop at the first hit. It's a breadth-first crawl that fetches each page once, strips it to text and runs Knuth–Morris–Pratt search across a pool of Web Workers, so pages are fetched and searched in parallel.

There's also rfind, a headless command-line version packaged as an AI agent skill. One call answers "which pages on this site mention X?" and returns only the matching pages with short snippets, with agent-safe defaults like a page cap and robots.txt support.
Get it on the Chrome Web Store →

screenshots.alt: Recursive Find in Chrome's side panel next to a Wikipedia article: searching 'texas' at depth 2 found 34 hits across 20 linked pages, each with highlighted snippets.

projects.title: PiDrone
projects.summary: An autonomous quadcopter that students build from scratch in Brown's intro robotics course, with state estimation, localization and SLAM running onboard on a Raspberry Pi.
body: PiDrone is the quadcopter students build from a kit and program to fly on their own in Brown's intro robotics course, taught by Stefanie Tellex. Its brain is a Raspberry Pi running ROS, with a downward-facing camera, a range sensor and an IMU.

In summer 2018 I was one of four undergraduates on a research team (funded by a Karen T. Romer UTRA) that took the first version of the course and rebuilt it. We extended the drone's capabilities and reworked the assignments based on feedback from the first class. The core of it was autonomy that runs entirely onboard, in Python: an Unscented Kalman Filter that turns noisy sensor data into an accurate state estimate, plus Monte Carlo localization and FastSLAM so the drone can map a room and know where it is in it.

We tested each piece against motion-capture ground truth and published the framework as Advanced Autonomy on a Low-Cost Educational Drone Platform, which I presented at IROS 2019 in Macau. Brown News covered the project that summer.
I also helped write the original Duckiesky curriculum, which brought the drone to high school students: build guides, lessons on sensing, and lesson plans for the teachers running it.
Photos: Nick Dentamaro / Brown University.

projects.title: Balsa Bridge
projects.summary: A balsa truss arch bridge that won my class's competition for the highest load-to-weight ratio.
body: A balsa truss arch bridge that won my class's competition for the highest load-to-weight ratio.

I built a truss arch from balsa sticks and reinforced every joint with paper gussets so the load spread into the members instead of tearing the glue joints apart. On test day we loaded it from a hanger under the deck until it failed. It held the most weight for its own weight of any bridge in the class.

housePrints.title: Bike Rack
housePrints.summary: A wall-mounted bike rack designed to go up with no tools: 3D-printed mounts hung on 3M Claw drywall hooks, with dowels pinned in place like a truss.
body: A wall-mounted bike rack designed to go up with no tools: 3D-printed mounts hung on 3M Claw drywall hooks, with dowels pinned in place like a truss.

The goal was a rack anyone could install without a drill. The 3D-printed mounts hang on 3M Claw hooks, and two wooden dowels angle out from them to cradle the bike's frame. I sketched the forces first, then modeled the mounts in Fusion 360.

Instead of fixing the dowels rigidly, I held them with pins and ribbon. The bike's frame rests right at the joint where the dowels meet, so the rack works like a truss: each member only carries push or pull along its length, and the joints don't have to resist bending.
Over time the Claw hooks kept working loose under the bike's weight, so a later version switched to screws.
